mcqs.question: Which statement best describes transport-layer head-of-line blocking in HTTP/2 over TCP?
options: Each HTTP/2 stream opens its own TCP connection, so a lost segment only affects that stream
A single lost TCP segment stalls delivery of all multiplexed HTTP/2 streams on that connection, because TCP enforces strict in-order byte delivery
It only happens when using HTTP/1.1, not HTTP/2
It's caused by HPACK's dynamic table growing too large
mcqs.explanation: TCP's in-order delivery is the root cause — one lost segment blocks every stream sharing that connection. HTTP/2 streams share a single TCP connection, not one each; this is specifically an HTTP/2-over-TCP problem, unrelated to HPACK.

mcqs.question: What lets QUIC avoid transport-layer head-of-line blocking that TCP has?
options: QUIC uses TCP under the hood but adds a caching layer
QUIC disables congestion control entirely, so packets are never delayed
QUIC tracks reliability, ordering, and loss recovery per-stream instead of per-connection, so a lost packet only affects its own stream
QUIC opens a separate UDP socket per stream
mcqs.explanation: Per-stream loss recovery is the actual mechanism. QUIC still does congestion control (redesigned, not disabled), doesn't run on top of TCP, and multiplexes streams within one UDP-based connection rather than opening a socket per stream.

mcqs.question: Why doesn't QUIC use 0-RTT for every request, even though it's faster?
options: Browsers don't support 0-RTT yet
0-RTT is only supported on the very first connection a client ever makes
0-RTT requires disabling encryption for that request
Data sent before the handshake completes can be captured and replayed by an attacker, so 0-RTT is restricted to requests safe to repeat (idempotent)
mcqs.explanation: The replay-attack risk on unauthenticated early data is the real constraint, so 0-RTT is limited to idempotent requests. 0-RTT actually requires a prior connection (resumption), not the first one, and stays encrypted.

mcqs.question: Why can QUIC survive a client's IP address changing mid-connection (e.g. Wi-Fi to cellular), while TCP cannot?
options: QUIC identifies a connection by a connection ID independent of IP/port, while TCP identifies it by the IP/port 4-tuple
QUIC connections don't use IP addresses at all
TCP automatically detects IP changes and reroutes without dropping the connection
QUIC re-runs the TLS handshake every time an IP changes, masking the switch
mcqs.explanation: The connection ID is the specific mechanism enabling migration. QUIC still runs over IP/UDP; TCP has no built-in IP-change tolerance (that's precisely the gap QUIC fills); and migration is designed to avoid a full handshake redo.

mcqs.question: Which of these is something QUIC changes relative to HTTP/2, beyond just moving to UDP?
options: It removes the need for encryption on the connection
It redefines congestion control and loss recovery to operate per-stream rather than per-connection
It eliminates the concept of HTTP streams entirely
It requires HTTP methods and status codes to change
mcqs.explanation: Per-stream loss recovery and congestion control is a genuine redesign beyond a transport swap. QUIC mandates encryption (doesn't remove it), keeps the concept of streams (just makes them more independent), and preserves HTTP semantics unchanged.
